common_name: Monsignor Intermediate Bearded Iris (Historic 1907 Violet Self Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in late summer to early fall so roots establish before frost, leaving the top of the rhizome exposed to sun.

directions: Introduced by the French nursery Vilmorin-Andrieux in 1907, this intermediate bearded iris carries deep hortense-violet standards over velvety mulberry-purple falls with darker veining toward the haft, all set off by a dense, orange-tipped beard. It is a vigorous grower with lax yellow-green foliage and freely produced bloom stalks that make a strong mass of color in the border. Lift and divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep it flowering well.

common_name: Mrs. Horace Darwin Intermediate Bearded Iris (Historic 1888 White-and-Violet Veined Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to sun so roots establish before frost.

directions: Raised in England by Sir Michael Foster and introduced in 1888, this intermediate bearded iris bears a white ground netted with reddish-lavender veining on the standards and clear violet veining on the falls, centered by a fine white beard tipped yellow. Its blooms are fragrant and well-rounded on branched, medium-height stalks, and the foliage is a lax, glaucous blue-green. It is often confused with the related 'Mrs. George Darwin' but shows only purple haft veining rather than amber. Divide every three to four years after flowering to maintain vigor.

common_name: Pallida Dalmatica Bearded Iris (Historic Pre-1597 Fragrant Dalmatian Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in late summer to early fall so roots establish before frost, leaving the rhizome top exposed to sun.

directions: Native to the Dalmatian coast and documented as early as John Gerard's 1597 Herball, this old clone of Iris pallida carries sword-shaped grey-green leaves and tall, sparsely branched stalks of pale lavender-blue flowers with yellow beards. The blooms carry a sweet, grape-like fragrance strong enough to scent a whole border, and the rhizomes are the traditional source of orris root used in perfumery after a long curing period. Grow in lean, well-drained soil and divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Queen of May Tall Bearded Iris (Historic Pre-1859 Rosy-Lavender Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in late summer to early fall with the top exposed to sun so roots establish before frost.

directions: Introduced in England by John Salter before 1859, this tall bearded iris was among the earliest cultivars to bring a true pink cast into iris breeding, showing a soft, luminous rosy-lavender self with a yellow, orange-tipped beard rather than the blue-violet shades typical of its era. It earned a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Merit in 1891 and went on to influence later generations of orchid-pink bearded iris. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep plants vigorous.
